1DiagramFigure 1.1: Subgroups of \(S_{3}\).
2DiagramFigure 1.2: Subgroups of \(S_{3}\), combining conjugate subgroups.
3DiagramFigure 1.3: Group chain for the Galois group \(S_{2}\) of the general quadratic equation.
4DiagramFigure 1.4: Group chain for the Galois group \(S_{3}\) of the general cubic equation.
5DiagramFigure 1.5: Group chain for the Galois group \(S_{4}\) of the general quartic equation.
6DiagramFigure 2.1: Every point \(p\) on a sphere \(S^{2}\) is surrounded by an open neighborhood that is indistinguishable from an open neighborhood of any point in the plane \(R^{2}\). Locally the two spaces are indistinguishable. Globally they are distinguishable.
7DiagramFigure 2.2: Every matrix in \(S L(2 ; \mathbb{R})\) can be written as the product of a symmetric matrix and a rotation matrix, both unimodular. The symmetric matrix is parameterized by a two-dimensional manifold, the two-sheeted hyperboloid \(z^{2}-x^{2}-y^{2}=1\). The rotation matrix is parameterized by a point on a circle. The parameterization manifold, \(H^{2} \times S^{1}\), is three dimensional.
8DiagramFigure 3.1: Structure of the matrix groups defined by linear constraints.
9DiagramFigure 3.2: The potentials to the left and right of the interaction region are constant, with \(V_{L}=V_{R}\). The wavefunctions to the left and right of this region are represented in the form \(\psi_{\sigma}(x)=A_{\sigma} e^{+i k x}+B_{\sigma} e^{-i k x}\), where \(\sigma=L, R\).
10DiagramFigure 3.3: Two potentials on the line are characterized by their \(T\) and \(S\) matrices.
11DiagramFigure 4.1: Standard forms into which a representation can be reduced.
12DiagramFigure 5.1: Structure of the matrix algebras for groups defined by linear constraints.
13DiagramFigure 6.1: Identification of the angular momentum operators with operators for two boson modes simplifies computation of the angular momentum matrix elements.
14DiagramFigure 7.1: "Light cone" for \(S L(2 ; \mathbb{R})\).
15DiagramFigure 7.2: (a) Two-sheeted and (b) single-sheeted hyperboloids. Both are quotients (coset spaces) of \(S L(2 ; \mathbb{R})\) by one of its two inequivalent types of subgroups, \(S O(2)\) and \(S O(1,1)\).
16DiagramFigure 7.3: Cartan's covering theorem. There is a unique correspondence between Lie algebras \(\mathfrak{g}\) and simply connected Lie groups \(S G=\bar{G}\). Every other Lie group with this Lie algebra is a quotient of the universal covering group by one of the discrete invariant subgroups \(D_{i}\) of \(\bar{G}\).

18DiagramFigure 8.1: Structure of the regular representation for different types of Lie algebras.
19Diagram
20DiagramFigure 8.2: Structure of nilpotent and solvable algebras.

22Diagram
23DiagramFigure 9.1: Coefficients in the secular equation are expressed in terms of the fully antisymmetric Levi-Civita tensor on \(n\) symbols.
24DiagramFigure 9.2: Invariant operators \(\phi_{j}(X)\) expressed in terms of the fully antisymmetric Levi-Civita tensor on \(n\) symbols. The invariant operators are obtained by replacing the coordinates \(a^{r}{ }_{s}\) by the operators \(X^{r}{ }_{s}\) in the coefficients \(\phi_{j}\) of the secular equation. Here the general element in the Lie algebra is \(X=a_{s}^{r} X^{r}{ }_{s}\).
25DiagramFigure 9.3: If the operators \(X\) are antisymmetric, \(X^{r}{ }_{s}=-X^{s}{ }_{r}\), contractions in the expressions for the Casimir operators can be rearranged as shown.
26DiagramFigure 9.4: The six operators in the two-photon algebra can be organized according to their roots, which are eigenvalues of a secular equation. Two operators have zero root.
27DiagramFigure 9.5: \(\alpha\) chain containing \(\beta\). This chain is used to compute coefficients \(N_{\alpha, \beta}\) in commutators \(\left[E_{\alpha}, E_{\beta}\right]=N_{\alpha, \beta} E_{\alpha+\beta}\).
28Diagram
29DiagramFigure 9.6: Two-dimensional root space diagrams. Top: \(A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}\). Bottom: \(D_{2}, G_{2}\).
30DiagramFigure 9.7: Root space \(C_{2}\). The roots are expressed in terms of a Cartesian (orthogonal) set \(\mathbf{e}_{1}, \mathbf{e}_{2}\) and a fundamental set \(\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}\).
31DiagramFigure 10.1: Rank-three root space diagrams. Top: \(A_{3}, D_{3}\). Bottom: \(B_{3}, C_{3}\).
32DiagramFigure 10.2: Root spaces constructed by the building-up principle. There are four infinite series and five exceptional Lie algebras. The root spaces are organized by rank.
33DiagramFigure 10.3: The root space \(D_{2}\) consists of two orthogonal root subspaces. Both describe the rank-one algebra \(A_{1}\).
34DiagramFigure 10.4: Root space for \(G_{2}\). Fundamental roots are \(\alpha_{1}=\mathbf{e}_{1}-\mathbf{e}_{2}\) and \(\alpha_{2}=\) \(-\mathbf{e}_{1}+2 \mathbf{e}_{2}-\mathbf{e}_{3}\). All roots are orthogonal to \(\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{e}_{1}+\mathbf{e}_{2}+\mathbf{e}_{3}\).
35DiagramFigure 10.5: Disconnected Dynkin diagrams describe semisimple Lie algebras. Here the disconnected diagram describes \(G_{2} \oplus B_{3}\).
36DiagramFigure 10.6: A simple linear chain can be removed. If the original is an allowed Dynkin diagram, the shortened diagram is also an allowed Dynkin diagram. In this case the original diagram is not an allowed Dynkin diagram.

41DiagramFigure 11．1．Lie groups \(S L(2 ; \mathbb{R})\) and \(S U(2)\) are related by analytic continuation． The canonical form for the diagonal and shift operators in their Lie algebras is also shown．
42DiagramFigure 11.2: The integer lattice in two dimensions carries representations of the algebras \(\mathfrak{s u}(2)\) and \(\mathfrak{s u}(1,1)\) that exponentiate to unitary irreducible representations with careful choice of the basis set. All points in this plane are mapped to other points along diagonals of the form \(n_{1}+n_{2}=\) constant. The subspaces of basis vectors for the unitary irreducible representations of \(S U(2)\) and \(S U(1,1)\) are separated by a "no man's land" defined by \(-1<n_{1}<0\) and \(-1<n_{2}<0\) (wavy lines). All points labeled \(x\) belong to the principal series of representations of \(S U(1,1)\) with \(n_{1}+n_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}+i \beta\).
